Near Threatened: Species that are close to being classified as Vulnerable. 7. Least Concern: Species that are not currently at risk of extinction. 8. Data Deficient: Species for which there is insufficient information to make an assessment of their risk of extinction. 9. Not Evaluated: Used for species that have not yet been assessed by the IUCN This category does not indicate that a species is not at risk of extinction, but simply that the species has not yet been studied enough to assign it to a category.

The objective of designing the red list is: i.to raise awareness about the level of risk to biodiversity. ii.to document and recognize species highly susceptible to extinction. iii.to develop strategies for the conservation of endangered species. iv.to disseminate information on global agreements, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity and Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) with awareness campaigns conducted by the government and concerned agencies. What is IUCN? The International Union for the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (IUCN), founded in 1948 and headquartered in Morges, Switzerland, is a prominent international institution dedicated to the sustainable use and conservation of biodiversity. Renamed IUCN-The World Conservation Union in 1990, it boasts over 70 member organizations, encompassing both governmental and nongovernmental agencies. With a panel comprising more than 5,000 experts, the IUCN collaborates with influential institutions like the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, UNESCO, and others. Recognized for its unique position, the IUCN serves as a key provider of technical advice on biodiversity issues.
